extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claims are directed to abstract ideas (Alice/Mayo) and whether claims recite or amount to an improvement in computer-functionality or other technology. Includes categories of judicially-identified abstract ideas and examples of claims that are and are not directed to abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must disclose and reflect an improvement to technology
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should disclose sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement, and the claim itself must reflect the improvement in technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important considerations: whether the claim covers a particular technical solution or way to achieve a desired outcome rather than merely claiming the idea of a solution; whether the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) is limited to computer implementation. See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for further principles and examples. Case guidance: a claimed process that can be performed without a computer cannot be characterized as an improvement in a computer (Synopsys, Inc. v. Mentor Graphics Corp., 839 F.3d 1138 (Fed. Cir. 2016)). Mere automation of manual processes or increasing speed solely from a general-purpose computer's capabilities is not sufficient (FairWarning IP v. Iatric Sys., 839 F.3d 1089; Credit Acceptance Corp. v. Westlake Services, 859 F.3d 1044). Claims that are only conventional implementations on generic components are also insufficient to show an improvement (Affinity Labs v. DirecTV; TLI Communications v. AV Auto.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere automation or conventional computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere automation of manual processes, increasing speed solely due to a general-purpose computer, or implementing conventional activity on generic computer components does not show an improvement in computer-functionality or other technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: FairWarning IP, Credit Acceptance, Affinity Labs, TLI Communications. Examiners should look beyond mere use of computer components to determine whether the claim adds a technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve improvement question early in Alice/Mayo analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are encouraged to resolve whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology as early as possible in the eligibility analysis (Step 2A or 2B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that is directed to a clear improvement (e.g., Enfish) could be found eligible at Pathway A (streamlined Step 2A) or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea. Even if an improvement is not clear enough for Step 2A, it may still contribute to eligibility in Step 2B as part of the inventive concept analysis. See Amdocs v. Openet for an example where an unconventional distributed network architecture contributed to eligibility at Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must recite the abstract idea to be directed to it
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is based on or involves an abstract idea but does not recite (set forth or describe) anything similar to a judicially-identified abstract idea, then the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2A requires a claim to recite an abstract idea in order to be directed to that idea. Judicial decisions: Enfish (self-referential table was based on but not directed to an abstract idea), DDR Holdings (modifying hyperlink protocol not directed to abstract idea), Trading Techs. (graphical UI improvement not directed). Non-limiting hypothetical examples of claims that do not set forth an abstract idea: a printer with mechanical components; a washing machine with controller; an earring glucose sensor with memory; a BRCA1 sequencing PCR method; a BIOS loading method that transfers BIOS from remote memory to local volatile memory and transfers control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim that recites an abstract idea may nonetheless be directed to an improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites an abstract idea, but the claim as a whole is directed to an improvement (or otherwise clearly does not seek to tie up the abstract idea), then the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of additional elements demonstrating an improvement can shift the focus from the abstract idea to a technical improvement. Types of improvements courts have recognized and cases: McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial animation), Enfish (self-referential table improvement), Research Corporation (blue noise mask plus steps that improved computer functioning). Non-limiting hypothetical examples: surgical shears with pressure regulator to limit force; robotic arm assembly with sensor and control for smooth motion; autofocus camera with algorithm and drive mechanism; internal combustion engine with exhaust gas recirculation controlled by a processor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on concepts identified in cases, not judicial descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claimed concept is similar to a concept the courts have identified as an abstract idea, examiners should rely on the concepts identified in the cases rather than the judicial descriptors themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associations between concepts and judicial descriptors (e.g., 'fundamental economic practices') are not mutually exclusive and some concepts may map to multiple descriptors (e.g., hedging in Bilski). Use the case law concepts as the analytic anchor rather than labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Fundamental economic practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to the economy and commerce—agreements between people, financial transactions, underwriting, price optimization, hedging, and similar foundational economic concepts—are examples courts have identified as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases/examples: buySAFE (transaction performance guaranty), OIP Technologies (offer-based price optimization), Bilski (hedging), Credit Acceptance (processing application for financing), In re Smith (rules for wagering games).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Concepts relating to mitigating risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts for mitigating risks (e.g., intermediated settlement or settlement risk mitigation) have been identified as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank (claims to intermediated settlement and creating 'shadow' account records were held directed to the abstract idea of intermediated settlement). Other examples include financial instruments designed to hedge risk (In re Chorna).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Methods of organizing human activity (managing relationships/transactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain methods of organizing human activity—managing relationships or transactions between people, satisfying or avoiding legal obligations, and similar interpersonal transactional activities—can be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases/examples: buySAFE (transaction guaranty), Dealertrack (managing credit application via forwarding to funding sources), Bancorp (managing life insurance policies with calculations). Other examples: arbitration (In re Comiskey), generating menus on a computer (Apple v. Ameranth), rule-based insurance claim processing (Accenture v. Guidewire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Methods of organizing human activity (advertising, marketing, sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to advertising, marketing, and sales activities or behaviors have been identified as abstract ideas in case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Apple v. Ameranth (menu-generation and transmitting as adding conventional computer components to known business practices). Other examples: structuring sales forces (In re Ferguson), using advertising as an exchange (Ultramercial), algorithms for scheduling business representative visits (In re Maucorps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Methods of organizing human activity (managing human behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts that manage human behavior—such as budgeting/notification systems, filtering content, or mental processes for diagnostics—may be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases/examples: Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One (tracking financial transactions against preset limits/budgeting), BASCOM (content filtering was considered an abstract idea under step 2A though later analysis affected outcome), In re Meyer (mental process used by a neurologist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Tracking or organizing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts related to tracking, filtering, or organizing information (data organization/processing) are commonly treated as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: BASCOM Global Internet v. AT&T Mobility (content filtering on an Internet network described as a method of organizing human behavior and an abstract idea). Courts have repeatedly characterized information organization and processing concepts in this category as abstract.
